fn-anon-limited.title: Functions with no key, guarded only by network rules
fn-anon-limited.why: Only callers from allowed networks can reach these functions, which lowers the risk. But anyone on those networks can call them with no key or sign-in, so the network rules are the only lock.
steps: Check first: review the app's access restriction rules (IP allow and deny rules) under Settings > Networking, or its private endpoint (a private network address). Confirm each allowed network still needs to call these functions.
Make sure the unmatched rule action (what happens to unlisted traffic) is Deny. If it is Allow, everyone not on a deny rule still gets in.
If the app uses a private endpoint, make sure public network access is turned off. A private endpoint alone does not block public traffic.

Watch for broad rules. A rule for a service tag (a named group of Azure IPs), such as Azure Front Door, lets in traffic from any instance of that service. To allow only yours, also filter on the HTTP header (a label sent with each request) that carries your instance ID.

Add a second lock: set authLevel (the function's key setting) to function, or turn on App Service authentication (built-in sign-in for the app). Tell callers first, because they will need the key or a sign-in.

fn-anon-auth.title: Functions with no key that rely on sign-in
fn-anon-auth.why: Callers must sign in through App Service authentication (built-in sign-in for the app) before these functions run. That blocks strangers. But by default, any user in your Entra ID tenant (your organization's user directory) can get a sign-in token for it.
steps: Check first: in the function app, open Settings > Authentication and confirm that requests without a sign-in are rejected or sent to sign-in, not let through.
Limit who can sign in. Set up the app's registration in Entra ID so only the users or groups that need it are allowed, or check user roles in the code. Test a real caller before and after.
These functions depend on that one setting. If someone turns authentication off, they become open to anyone, so consider also setting authLevel (the function's key setting) to function.

app-config-unread.title: App settings could not be read
app-config-unread.why: The tool could not read this app's settings. So it could not check the TLS version (how traffic is encrypted), FTP (an old file upload method), remote debugging or network rules. Any of those problems could be hiding here.
steps: Make sure the account the assessment uses can read the app. Open the app and go to Access control (IAM) > Check access. Look for a role such as Reader (read-only access to resources) on the app, its resource group or the subscription.
Run the assessment again. A one-time error can also cause this.

Until the tool can read it, check the settings by hand. Under Settings > Configuration > General settings, look at the minimum TLS version, FTP state and remote debugging. Under Settings > Networking, look at the access restrictions.

app-https-off.title: Apps do not force HTTPS
app-https-off.why: These apps still answer over plain HTTP (unencrypted web traffic). Anything sent that way, such as passwords, keys or business data, can be read or changed by someone on the network path.
steps: Check first: find callers that still use http:// addresses, such as scripts, webhooks (automatic web calls) or other apps, and change them to https://. A caller that cannot follow a redirect will fail after the change.
If the app uses its own domain name, make sure that domain has a certificate binding (a certificate attached to the domain) first. It shows as Secured under Settings > Custom domains.
In the portal, open the app, go to Settings > Configuration > General settings, turn on HTTPS Only, and save the change.
Test the app over HTTPS and confirm the callers still work.
If App Service authentication (built-in sign-in for the app) is on, it redirects requests to HTTPS by default. Turn on HTTPS Only anyway, so this does not depend on that setting.

app-tls-old.title: Apps accept old TLS versions
app-tls-old.why: TLS (the encryption for web traffic) versions 1.0 and 1.1 are old and no longer considered secure. Allowing them makes it easier for an attacker to read or tamper with traffic to the app.
steps: Check first: ask the app owner which systems call the app. Old clients, devices or scripts that only support TLS 1.0 or 1.1 will fail to connect after the change, so update them first.
In the portal, open the app and go to Settings > Configuration > General settings. Set the minimum inbound TLS version to 1.2, or 1.3 if every caller supports it, and save the change.
The SCM site (the app's deployment tools site) has its own minimum TLS version. Check it too.
To catch apps that slip back, use the built-in Azure Policy (automatic rule checking) named 'App Service apps should use the latest TLS version'.

links.title: What is TLS/SSL in Azure App Service?

app-ftp.title: Apps allow plain FTP deployments
app-ftp.why: Plain FTP (an old file upload method) sends the deployment user name, password and files without encryption. Anyone who captures them can upload their own code to the app.
steps: Check first: ask the app owner how they deploy. To see real use, send the app's AppServiceAuditLogs (the log of deployment sign-ins) to Azure Monitor (the Azure logging service) and look for FTP sign-ins.

In the portal, open the app, go to Settings > Configuration > General settings, and under Platform settings set FTP state to FTPS only (FTP with encryption). If nobody uses FTP, choose Disabled. Select Save.
FTPS only needs a minimum inbound TLS version (the encryption level) of 1.2 or higher, so check that setting on the same page.

If nobody deploys with FTP, also set FTP Basic Auth Publishing Credentials (user name and password sign-in) to Off on the same page. Then use a deployment method that signs in with Entra ID (your organization's user directory).

links.title: Deploy your app to Azure App Service using FTP/S

app-remote-debug.title: Remote debugging left on
app-remote-debug.why: Remote debugging lets a developer connect a debugging tool to the live app. It is meant for short troubleshooting sessions; left on, it is one more way into a production app.
steps: Check first: ask the app owner if someone is debugging right now. If so, agree on when they will finish.
In the portal, open the app, go to Settings > Configuration > General settings, turn off remote debugging in the Debugging section, and save the change.
This setting should turn off by itself after 48 hours. If you keep finding it on, find out who or what turns it back on, such as a deployment script or template.

app-open-ip.title: Apps reachable from any IP address
app-open-ip.why: Anyone on the internet can reach these apps. That is normal for a public website. For an internal API or Function App, the app's own key or sign-in is then the only thing keeping strangers out.
steps: Check first: decide with each app owner if the app is meant to be public. If it is a public website, no change is needed; record that decision.
For internal APIs and Function Apps, list who must reach the app, such as office networks, partners and other Azure services, so real callers are not locked out.
Add allow rules under Settings > Networking > Public network access, then select Save. By default, once you add one rule, all traffic not on the list is denied.
Set rules for the SCM site (the app's deployment tools site) too, or select Use main site rules.
If only internal systems call the app, add a private endpoint (a private network address) and then turn off public network access.

links.title: Set up Azure App Service access restrictions

logicapp-open-trigger.title: Logic App HTTP triggers open to any IP
logicapp-open-trigger.why: The trigger URL (the address that starts the workflow) holds a SAS (a signed secret in the URL). Anyone who has the full URL can start the workflow from anywhere. These URLs can end up in scripts, tickets and emails, and the workflow runs with all the access its connections have.
steps: Check first: for each workflow, list every system that calls its trigger URL and the IP addresses it calls from. Any caller you miss will be blocked.

Consumption logic apps (run on shared hosting): open the logic app, go to Settings > Workflow settings, and under Allowed inbound IP addresses choose Specific IP ranges. Enter the callers' ranges. If only a parent workflow calls it through the built-in Azure Logic Apps action, choose Only other Logic Apps.
Standard logic apps (run on dedicated hosting): add access restriction rules (IP allow and deny rules) under Settings > Networking. It works the same way as for an App Service app.

For stronger control on Consumption logic apps, add an authorization policy (rules for which tokens are accepted) under Settings > Authorization. Include at least the Issuer and Audience claims (fields inside the token). Then move callers to sign-in tokens from Entra ID (your organization's user directory).

When all callers use tokens, disable SAS authentication through the REST API (a direct Azure management call). This stops every caller still using the old URL. Standard logic apps can use Easy Auth (built-in App Service sign-in) instead.
If a trigger URL may have been shared too widely, regenerate the access key (the secret behind the URLs) under Settings > Access Keys. All old URLs stop working, so give callers the new ones.

automation-runas.title: Automation accounts still use Run As connections
automation-runas.why: Runbooks (saved automation scripts) use this connection to sign in as an app registration (an app's identity in Entra ID). Run As accounts got Contributor (can change almost any resource) on the subscription by default, and anyone who edits runbooks here can use it. The Run As feature was retired on 30 September 2023.
steps: Check first: find which runbooks use the connection. Search the runbook code for Get-AutomationConnection and the connection name, or use the check scripts linked in the migration guide. Note the app registration (its application ID is stored in the connection) and every role it holds.

Turn on the Automation account's managed identity (an Azure sign-in with no secret) under Account Settings > Identity. Give it only the roles the runbooks need, not Contributor on the whole subscription.
Copy each runbook, change the copy to sign in with Connect-AzAccount -Identity, and test it. When it works, update the real runbook the same way.
Before deleting anything, confirm that no runbook still uses the connection and that recent jobs succeed with the managed identity.
Then remove the old app's role assignments under Access control (IAM) > Role assignments > Remove. Also remove the connection and its certificate from the Automation account.
Last, delete the app registration: in Entra ID, open App registrations, select the app, and select Delete on its Overview page.

apiconn-dormant.title: Connections run as an inactive user account
apiconn-dormant.why: This API connection (a saved sign-in a workflow uses) acts as a user who has not signed in successfully for 90 days or more. If that person left, the account may be unwatched but still have access. A connection that is used often usually shows recent sign-ins, so this one may also be unused or broken.
steps: Check first: find the workflows that use this connection and look at their recent run history. A logic app lists its connections under Development Tools > API connections, or under Workflows > Connections for Standard logic apps (the dedicated hosting type). Failed runs at steps that use this connection can mean it is already broken.

Look up the account in Entra ID (your organization's user directory) under Entra ID > Users, and check its sign-ins. Find out who owns it and whether it is a dedicated service account or a person's account.
If no workflow needs the connection anymore, agree with the workflow owner before you remove it.

If the workflow is still needed, sign the connection in again with a dedicated service account that has an owner. If that connection type supports it, use a managed identity (an Azure sign-in with no secret) instead. Then test the workflow.
Once the workflows run on the new account, review the old account and disable it if nothing else uses it.

apiconn-named.title: Connections tied to one person's account
apiconn-named.why: This API connection (a saved sign-in a workflow uses) acts with one person's access and in their name. It can stop working when they leave, change their password or lose access, and it may reach more than the workflow needs.
steps: Check first: list the workflows that use each connection and what they do, so you know what could break.
Get a dedicated service account with a named owner, and give it only the access the workflow needs in each target system.
Sign the connection in again with that account, or create a new connection with it and switch each workflow step to it. Test each workflow.

Where the connection type supports it, use a managed identity (an Azure sign-in with no secret) instead of any account. The documented examples are mostly Azure services, such as Blob Storage, Key Vault and SQL Server.

The Fin & Ops Apps (Dynamics 365) connection has no managed identity option, and its service principal (an app's own sign-in) option is listed but not supported. Use a dedicated service account for it.

manual.title: LCS roles can reveal VM admin passwords
manual.why: In Lifecycle Services (LCS, Microsoft's Finance and Operations project portal), anyone with the Project owner or Environment manager role can see the local account passwords for the project's cloud-hosted VMs (virtual machines). Microsoft says these passwords cannot be hidden from those two roles. A former contractor, or someone given the role by mistake, could use them to sign in to a development VM as an administrator.
steps: Sign in to Lifecycle Services and open each project. Select Project users from the menu or the Project users tile.

List everyone who has the Project owner or Environment manager role. Mark partner and vendor accounts, and anyone who left or changed jobs. Also list Operations users: that role can open the Cloud-hosted environments tool, and Microsoft does not say whether it can see the passwords. Repeat this list every quarter.
Check first: ask each person's manager if they still manage cloud-hosted environments. Keep at least two trusted Project owners from your own company so the project never loses its owner.
Change people who do not manage environments to Project team member. Microsoft says this role hides the local account passwords and cannot manage cloud-hosted environments.

Keep the number of Microsoft Entra tenant administrators small. Microsoft says they become LCS organization admins when they sign in and can add themselves as Project owner on any project the tenant owns.

If someone who could see the passwords has left, treat those passwords as known and plan with the environment owner to replace the VM. Microsoft says development environments are considered disposable. Until then, limit Remote Desktop to approved addresses (see the item on remote access to LCS development VMs).

Check first: confirm with the environment owner that all code is checked in to version control, that nothing else on the VM is still needed, and that no other cloud-hosted environment uses its virtual network. Microsoft says you cannot delete an environment while other environments use its virtual network.
Then, in LCS under Cloud-hosted environments, deallocate and delete the old environment, and deploy a new one.

manual.title: Unverified remote access to LCS development VMs
manual.why: Cloud-hosted environments from Lifecycle Services (LCS, Microsoft's Finance and Operations project portal) run in your own Azure subscription. Microsoft says Remote Desktop (port 3389) and the environment's web page (HTTPS, port 443) are open to any address by default, so anyone on the internet can try to sign in. If nobody owns the IP allow-list (list of approved network addresses), entries pile up and never get removed.
steps: For each cloud-hosted environment, open the Azure resource group that has the same name as the environment in LCS. Then open its network security group (the VM's firewall rules).

Write down how developers connect today: VPN (private link to the company network), an IP allow-list on the Remote Desktop rule (port 3389), or something else. Name the person who approves new addresses and where approvals are kept.

Check first: before you narrow a rule, collect the current public IP address of every developer, partner and system that connects, and agree on a test time. Leave the WinRM rule (port 5986) alone, even if a security scan says to close it: Microsoft says LCS uses it to set up and manage the VM and already limits it to LCS addresses. Keep outbound internet access open, because Microsoft says the apps need it.

Limit the Remote Desktop rule, and if you can the web (HTTPS, port 443) rule, to approved addresses only. Use Microsoft's allow-list rules for its own sandboxes as the model: no asterisk or zero entries, no wide ranges, no Azure datacenter ranges, and no public places such as coffee shops.

About Azure Bastion (an Azure service for Remote Desktop through the Azure portal, without opening the Remote Desktop port to the internet): Microsoft's FAQ says it has not tested or supported cloud-hosted environments with Bastion, although its one-box security page lists Bastion as an option to consider. If you try it, test on one VM first and keep another way in.
Review the allow-list with the approver every quarter. Remove entries for people and places that no longer need access, as Microsoft recommends.
